title: Etale lifts of permissible blowup charts with labelled strict transforms
statement:
Let $X$ be a Noetherian regular scheme [pqf-def-locnoeth, def-weil-regular-scheme], where Noetherian means locally Noetherian and quasi-compact. Let $B\subset X$ be a normal crossings divisor [def-trf-normal-crossings-divisor], and let $H\subset B$ be a reduced union of irreducible components [def-trf-union-of-irreducible-components] which is a strict normal crossings boundary [def-trf-strict-normal-crossings-boundary]. Let $M\subset B$ be a permissible center [def-trf-permissible-center]. Write $b:Y=\operatorname{Bl}_M(X)\to X$ [def-nagata-global-blowup], $E=(b^{-1}M)_{\mathrm{red}}$, $C=(b^{-1}B)_{\mathrm{red}}$, $D=(b^{-1}(H\cup M))_{\mathrm{red}}$ [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction], and let $H_a$ be exactly the distinct reduced irreducible components of $H$ [def-weil-irreducible-components]. Superscript $\mathrm{st}$ denotes scheme-theoretic strict transform [def-nagata-strict-transform]. For every $y\in E$, with $x=b(y)$, there exist an actual etale neighborhood $W\to X$ [def-weil-etale-morphism], $w\mapsto x$, an affine neighborhood $W^\circ$ of $w$, and an open subscheme $V\subset Y\times_X W^\circ$ containing a point $z$ above both $y$ and $w$, with the following properties. In $R=\mathcal O_{W,w}$ there are regular parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ [def-weil-pbc-regular-system-of-parameters] and sets $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$ and $\varnothing\ne J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ with $J\cap\{1,\ldots,r\}\ne\varnothing$, such that $B$, $H$, and $M$ pull back near $w$ to $V(t_1\cdots t_r)$, $V(\prod_{i\in I}t_i)$, and $V(t_j:j\in J)$, respectively. The components $H_a$ through $x$ correspond bijectively to $I$, and their pullbacks are the assigned single hyperplanes. For some $j\in J$, $\mathcal O_{V,z}$ is the localization at the point over $z$ of
$$R[u_i\mid i\in J\setminus\{j\}]/(t_i-t_j u_i\mid i\in J\setminus\{j\}).$$
The projection $V\to Y$ is etale. At $z$, $E$ pulls back to $V(t_j)$; each $H_a^{\mathrm{st}}$ pulls back either to the empty subscheme or to one distinct hyperplane, given by $u_i=0$ for its index $i\in I\cap(J\setminus\{j\})$, or by $t_i=0$ for $i\in I\setminus J$; index $j$ disappears. These are different from the exceptional hyperplane. The pullbacks of $C$ and $D$ are the reduced unions of the exceptional hyperplane with, respectively, all surviving boundary hyperplanes and the selected hyperplanes just described. The pullbacks of $B^{\mathrm{st}}$ and $H^{\mathrm{st}}$ are the corresponding unions with the exceptional hyperplane omitted. These assertions hold as germs of closed subschemes at $z$, equivalently after shrinking $V$ around $z$. The local ring at $z$ is regular, the hyperplanes through $z$ have equations among a regular system of parameters there, and each intersection of $s$ distinct such hyperplanes is empty or regular of codimension $s$. Empty $H$ is allowed.

source.place: Expose VIII 4.1.2--4.1.4(i), printed p. 117; Lemma 4.2.9 and its coordinate-chart proof, printed p. 121; the regular-intersection criterion is Remark 4.2.2(i), printed p. 118.

proof.text: Since $y\in E$, $x\in M$. Apply the coordinate clause of permissible center to obtain an actual etale $W\to X$, $w\mapsto x$, an affine neighborhood $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $w$, and sections representing a full regular parameter system of $R=A_{\mathfrak p}=\mathcal O_{W,w}$. Rename the boundary parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ and write the center parameters as $(t_i:i\in J)$, with $J\ne\varnothing$. The containment $M\subset B$ gives $t_1\cdots t_r\in\sqrt{(t_i:i\in J)}$ in $R$. By the regular-parameter quotient theorem, after permuting the full parameter system, $R/(t_i:i\in J)$ is regular local and is a domain (the latter also follows from the cited UFD theorem). If $J$ missed every boundary index, each $t_i$, $i\le r$, would be a nonzero member of a parameter system in this quotient, contradicting that their product is zero. Thus $J\cap\{1,\ldots,r\}\ne\varnothing$. Shrinking $U$ preserves all the defining equations.

source.place: VIII 4.1.2, printed p.117; boundary-contained specialization; regular-parameter quotient check

proof.text: The closed subscheme $H$ is Noetherian: affine closed charts are quotients of Noetherian rings, and a closed subset of a quasi-compact Noetherian space is quasi-compact. The finite-components theorem therefore makes its component family finite. The flat pullback of the effective Cartier ideal of $H$ is Cartier, and its closed subscheme is reduced because the map to $H$ is etale. In $R$ its ideal is therefore a principal radical ideal $(h)$, with $h\ne0$, and its support lies in $V(T)$, $T=\prod_{i=1}^r t_i$, because $|H|\subset|B|$ by the union-of-components hypothesis. Hence $T^N\in(h)$ for some $N$. Unique factorization in $R$ shows that $h$ is a unit times a product of the primes $t_i$ with exponents at most $N$; radicality makes every positive exponent one. Let $I$ be their set, allowing $I=\varnothing$ when $h$ is a unit. The scheme $W$ is locally Noetherian by the locally-Noetherian ascent theorem, since an etale morphism is locally of finite presentation and $X$ is locally Noetherian. The finite germ-spreading lemma, applied on $W$, makes the ideal equality $(h)=(\prod_{i\in I}t_i)$ hold on one affine neighborhood of $w$ together with the equations for $B,M$. Apply etale component-coordinate identification to $D=H$ with this sublist of the full parameter system: the components of $H$ are regular by the strict-boundary hypothesis. It gives the required bijection from components through $x$ to $I$, their scheme-theoretic single-hyperplane pullbacks, and empty pullbacks for components missing $x$. Shrink once more and call the resulting affine neighborhood $W^\circ$.

source.place: VIII Remark 4.2.2(i), printed p.118, and 4.2.9, printed p.121; factorization and component labelling

proof.text: There is a point $z_0\in Y\times_X W^\circ$ over the prescribed $y,w$: by the fibre-product-points theorem it suffices to take a prime of $\kappa(y)\otimes_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(w)$. This ring is nonzero, since tensoring nonzero vector spaces over a field is nonzero (extend $1$ to bases); a maximal ideal supplies a prime. The etale base-change theorem makes $Y\times_X W^\circ\to Y$ etale. The blowup preserved-open comparison, applied to the flat map $W^\circ\to X$, identifies this fibre product with the blowup of $M\times_XW^\circ$. The standard affine chart cover supplies $j\in J$ with $z_0$ in its $t_j$-chart. Take $V$ to be that open chart and $z=z_0$. The open-restriction theorem gives that $V\to Y$ is etale.

source.place: VIII Lemma 4.2.9 chart cover, printed p.121; Stacks 01JT (schemes.tex, lemma-points-fibre-product) and 0805 (divisors.tex, lemma-flat-base-change-blowing-up)

proof.text:
Write $K=(t_i:i\in J)\subset A$ using the representing sections. The ring of $V$ is $A[K/t_j]\subset A[1/t_j]$. Localizing its coefficients at $\mathfrak p$ gives $R[KR/t_j]$: both rings are generated by the same fractions $t_i/t_j$, and localization commutes with adjoining these fractions. Every element of $A\setminus\mathfrak p$ is a unit in $\mathcal O_{V,z}$ because $z$ maps to $w$. Thus $\mathcal O_{V,z}$ is exactly the localization of $R[KR/t_j]$ at the prime induced by $z$. Apply the permissible-coordinate-chart lemma over the regular local ring $R$ to identify this ring before the last localization with
$$A_j=R[u_i:i\in J\setminus\{j\}]/(t_i-t_ju_i:i\in J\setminus\{j\}).$$
The identification carries $u_i$ to the actual ratio on $V$. It gives regularity of $\mathcal O_{V,z}$ and, for the boundary hyperplanes of the chart, namely $t_j$, $u_i$ ($i\in(J\setminus\{j\})\cap\{1,\ldots,r\}$) and $t_k$ ($k\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\setminus J$), simultaneous distinct regular-parameter positions for those through $z$. Every hyperplane the item displays is among these, since $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$. The same lemma gives the regularity and codimension of their intersections at this prime, including intersections empty because one equation is a unit.

source.place: VIII Lemma 4.2.9 coordinate-chart computation, printed p.121

proof.text: Scheme-theoretic strict transforms may be compared with this local model as follows. For each $Z=B,H,H_a$, the strict transform is the closure of the inverse image of $Z$ off the center. The finite-center open-closure lemma gives a quasi-compact open immersion into this closure, scheme-theoretically dense there, and characterizes the closure uniquely by these properties and its agreement with the open. Under a flat base change this open remains scheme-theoretically dense by dense-flat-pullback. Its quasi-compactness persists: the preserved open is the complement of the same finite family of center equations, as the preserved-open diagram states. Applying the uniqueness clause of the open-closure lemma in the changed ambient closed subscheme identifies the pulled-back closure with the closure of that open. This applies first to $W^\circ\to X$ and then to coefficient localization $A\to R$, which is flat by the localization-flat theorem, and finally to localization at $z$. The preserved-open diagram identifies the blowups and the opens throughout. Consequently the strict transforms of $B,H,H_a$ have exactly their coordinate-model strict-transform ideals in $\mathcal O_{V,z}$; no topological-closure substitution or generic-point assumption is used.

For a selected component labelled $i\in I$, the coordinate-chart lemma now gives its strict transform as $V(u_i)$ when $i\in J\setminus\{j\}$, as empty when $i=j$, and as $V(t_i)$ when $i\notin J$. The component labels remain distinct by step 2 and the distinct parameter positions of step 4. In particular a surviving nonempty hyperplane is different from $V(t_j)$. For $B$ and $H$ themselves, the strict-transform closure of a finite union is the union of the individual closures scheme-theoretically: on an affine chart, its ideal is the kernel of restriction to the complement of the center, and the kernel for a finite union is the intersection of the individual kernels. Indeed, off the center the chart ring becomes $R[1/t_j]$, a localization of the UFD $R$, in which the ideal of the union $(\prod_k t_k)$ of the distinct prime equations equals the intersection $\bigcap_k(t_k)$; so a section vanishes in the localized quotient of the union exactly when it vanishes in every localized component quotient, that is, when it lies in every individual kernel. Thus the strict transforms are precisely the unions of all surviving boundary hyperplanes and of the selected surviving hyperplanes, respectively, omitting the exceptional hyperplane. Equivalently, this is the product of their distinct parameter equations, since in a UFD an element divisible by every distinct prime is divisible by their product.

source.place: VIII Lemma 4.2.9, printed p.121; finite intersections of closure-kernel ideals

proof.text: Reduction commutes here with etale pullback. In fact for any closed subscheme $Z\subset Y$, the pullback of $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ to $V$ is reduced by etale base change and the etale-reduced theorem, and has the same support as $Z\times_YV$; hence it is its reduction by the nilradical definition. In the local chart the center ideal extends to $(t_j)$, so the coordinate calculation gives $E=V(t_j)$. Substitution $t_i=t_ju_i$ for $i\in J\setminus\{j\}$ in $\prod_{i=1}^r t_i$ shows that the radical of the total boundary ideal is the product of $t_j$ and exactly the surviving boundary equations: $J$ meets the boundary indices, so a positive power of $t_j$ occurs. Similarly the support of the inverse image of $H\cup M$ is $V(t_j)$ together with precisely the selected surviving hyperplanes, even if $I=\varnothing$. These ideals are radical because their factors are distinct primes in the regular local UFD, so these are equalities of reduced closed subschemes, giving the asserted $C,D$.

source.place: VIII 4.1.2 and Lemma 4.2.9, printed pp.117,121; reduction via etale-reduced ascent

proof.text: All the assertions are germs at the same $z$ of the actual open chart $V$, not charts of a strict henselization. Sections defining the finitely many displayed hyperplanes are the actual ratios or original sections on $V$. The regular-parameter and intersection assertions at $z$ were supplied in step 4. Finally equality of any of the finitely many closed-subscheme germs with these models extends to a common neighborhood of $z$ by the finite germ-spreading lemma. Its hypotheses hold: etale morphisms are locally of finite type, $X$ is locally Noetherian, and the blowup chart is a finite-type algebra over a Noetherian affine neighborhood. The locally-Noetherian ascent theorem therefore applies to $W^\circ$ and its blowup charts. The empty family for $H$ and empty surviving strict transforms require no additional shrinking conditions.
